identity.title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?

problem.claim: Explain how aggregate power-law scaling in repeated-attempt language-model tasks can arise when each individual problem appears to improve exponentially with attempts.

gap.claim: Existing observations of aggregate polynomial scaling conflict with the per-problem exponential prediction, leaving the source of aggregate scaling unclear.

contributions.claim: Shows that per-problem exponential scaling can coexist with aggregate polynomial scaling when single-attempt success probabilities are heavy-tailed.
Uses the distribution of per-problem success probabilities to explain previously observed deviations from power-law scaling.
Provides a method for forecasting the power-law exponent with author-reported relative error reduced by an order of magnitude, or with approximately 2–4 orders of magnitude less inference compute.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their distributional perspective, which reconciles individual exponential scaling with aggregate polynomial scaling and supports scaling-exponent forecasting.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report empirically confirming that failure rates for individual problems fall exponentially with the number of attempts.
The authors report that a heavy-tailed distribution of single-attempt success probabilities produces aggregate power-law behavior despite per-problem exponential scaling.
The authors report substantially more accurate exponent forecasting or equivalent inference-compute savings, with the stated approximate ranges.

narrative_sequence.summary: Repeated-attempt evaluations across mathematical, proof-assistant, and multimodal-jailbreaking tasks show aggregate power-law scaling.
A simple calculation predicts exponential decline in each problem’s failure rate, apparently conflicting with aggregate polynomial scaling.
A heavy-tailed distribution of per-problem success probabilities reconciles the two scaling behaviors, with very difficult tasks shaping the aggregate trend.
The same perspective is reported to explain deviations from power laws and improve exponent forecasting or reduce inference compute.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates per-problem scaling from aggregate scaling and attributes their apparent conflict to heterogeneity in single-attempt success probabilities.

lessons.interpretation: Disaggregating outcomes before fitting an aggregate law can reveal whether task-population heterogeneity drives the observed trend.
lessons.application: When reporting a scaling law, analyze both per-instance curves and the distribution of instance-level success probabilities, then state how aggregation affects the fitted exponent.
lessons.exception: This move is unsuitable when instance-level probabilities cannot be estimated reliably or when the evaluation target is inherently aggregate.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, sample sizes, fitting procedures, or uncertainty estimates.
The claimed error reduction and compute savings lack quantitative baselines and experimental conditions in the supplied text.
The abstract does not establish that the proposed forecasting method generalizes beyond the task families mentioned.
